title: Test Your Understanding: System Diagrams and Trade-offs
description: Layering, sync vs async conventions, annotations, and what makes a diagram useful in reviews and interviews.

questions.question: What is the main problem with a 'component theater' diagram?

options.text: It uses too many colors and icons
It lists services but hides behavior, failure modes, and trade-offs
It always has too few boxes for a production system
It can only be used for monoliths, not microservices

questions.explanation: Component theater shows what exists without explaining data paths, sync vs async boundaries, or degradation under failure — the questions design reviews and interviews actually ask.

questions.question: Which diagram layer is best for answering 'What happens when the cache cluster in AZ-a goes down?'

options.text: Context diagram
High-level tier diagram only
Failure boundaries layer with degradation notes
Vendor architecture reference diagram

questions.explanation: Failure boundaries group components that share fate and show how the system degrades — e.g. bypass cache, fail over AZ, or queue locally — when a dependency is unavailable.

questions.question: In the solid vs dashed arrow convention described in the post, what does a dashed arrow from API to Queue typically mean?

options.text: The API waits for the queue to confirm the message before responding
The call is fire-and-forget; the user path does not wait for downstream processing
The connection is encrypted
The queue is the source of truth for reads

questions.explanation: Dashed arrows mark asynchronous boundaries — enqueue and move on. Solid arrows mark synchronous request/response where latency accumulates on the caller's critical path.

questions.question: Which annotations belong on a strong system design diagram? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Per-operation consistency choice (e.g. stale reads OK for 60s)
Every microservice's programming language
Latency budget on the hot path (e.g. p99 50ms)
Degradation behavior when a dependency fails

questions.explanation: Short labels for consistency, latency, and failure behavior tie the diagram to requirements and trade-offs. Implementation trivia like language choice rarely helps at design level.

questions.question: You're diagramming cache-aside reads and async search indexing. What is the clearest approach?

options.text: One diagram with every component connected to every other component
Separate read (solid) and write/index (dashed after enqueue) flows with role labels on cache, DB, and index
Omit the queue so the diagram stays minimal
Draw only the database since it is the source of truth

questions.explanation: Splitting read vs write/index paths avoids arrow soup. Role labels (cache = fast optional reads, DB = source of truth, index = derived) keep the story clear without extra boxes.

questions.question: On a first-pass high-level diagram, you should include every Redis replica and Kafka partition so the diagram is complete.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Start with one box per role (cache, queue, DB). Add replicas and partitions when failure boundaries or read scaling is the topic — not on the first pass.

questions.question: In a system design interview, what should you do before drawing internal services?

options.text: Draw all microservices so the interviewer sees you know the stack
Confirm scope with a context diagram and identify the hot path from requirements/math
Copy a reference architecture from a cloud provider
Start with the database schema

questions.explanation: Context and scope prevent wasted depth. The hot path (often read-heavy) should drive the first data-flow diagram; services split only when boundaries matter.

questions.question: In the before/after example, what makes the 'after' diagram stronger?

options.text: It has more boxes and arrows
It exposes read vs write paths, async indexing, and explicit cache-failure degradation
It removes the database to simplify
It uses dashed lines for all arrows

questions.explanation: The improved diagram tells a behavioral story: cache-aside reads, sync write to DB, async index build, and known behavior when cache is down — not just more components.
